summary_for_principal: Added the part of the engine that decides which way a process branches, and the part that stops a loop running forever. Both are small, pure pieces of logic: given the current facts about a run, they answer one question each (which path fires; has this loop been taken too many times) without touching anything else. The important property this step protects: if a routing decision genuinely has nowhere to go (which should never happen, but a badly written definition could still produce it), the engine stops and says so, rather than guessing and carrying on — the exact mistake found in the old, unused engine earlier in this work. Nothing here is wired up to actually run a process yet; that is the final step.

also.reason: Re-confirmed the exact defect (default to first route on no match) this step's evaluate_route() is built to defeat, rather than relying on memory of it from an earlier turn.
Confirmed the exact constant names/values (LOOP_BUDGET=10, LOOP_ON_EXHAUSTED=ESCALATED) before citing them in check_loop_budget, rather than restating the defaults from memory.

interpretation.ask_as_given: Continue WP-02 autonomously, PR by PR — this run picks up step 3 (ROUTE execution + loop budgets) of the 5-step sequence.
interpretation.read_as: Build route evaluation and loop-budget checking as pure functions of state already resolved by the caller, following the same scoping pattern step 2 used for attempt_step: do the one well-specified thing this step owns, and leave what needs the whole Process graph or durable records (loop reachability, the actual counters) to next()/report() in step 5.

decisions.headline: Loop reachability (which routes are loops) and the durable taken-count are next()/report()'s job, not routes.py's.
decisions.problem: check_loop_budget needs to know how many times a loop has already been taken this run scope (S7.3: "rebuilt from durable records"), which requires reading RecordsPort and knowing the Process graph's structure (a loop is defined by reachability back to an earlier node) — neither of which routes.py has.
options_rejected: Give check_loop_budget a RecordsPort and have it compute the taken-count itself: rejected — this would mean the function is no longer a pure function of its inputs, breaking the same easily-tested-unit property attempt_step (step 2) was deliberately built to have, and would require routes.py to also know about run/scope/node addressing it currently has no reason to know.
decisions.cost_to_change: None expected to be needed — this mirrors step 2's own attempt_step/caller split exactly, and that split has already proven itself once.

evidence.claim: Spec S7.3 defines a loop by graph reachability ("any route ... whose target can reach the node it leaves from") and its counter as "rebuilt from durable records" — both properties of the whole Process graph plus RecordsPort, not of a single route in isolation.

decisions.revisit_if: Step 5 (next/report/decide) finds this split awkward once it actually has to call both functions together — not expected, but the two are stacked PRs specifically so this could still be revisited before either merges.

lessons.maxim: The expression grammar's string literals are double-quoted only (spec S8's `literal := string | ...`, tokenizer regex requires `".."`); a test fixture written with Python single-quoted strings containing single-quoted expression literals will parse in Python but fail at DefinitionError when the expression is actually parsed.
lessons.incident: First draft of tests/engine/test_routes.py wrote `if_="state.verdict == 'A'"` (single quotes inside a double-quoted Python string) — every route test failed with `[V5] unexpected character "'"` until the literals were rewritten as `if_='state.verdict == "A"'`.
lessons.destination: Any future test in this repository that constructs an expression string literal — use double quotes for the expression's own string literals, single-quoted (or escaped double-quoted) Python strings to hold them.
lessons.proposed_check: tests/engine/test_routes.py's own passing suite now exercises this correctly.
